name: The Tree of the Changes — the books of the I Ching
description: The history of the I Ching as a family tree of books, one book per node: from numbers on bone, through the Zhouyi, the Ten Wings and the Han canon, the commentators who read it for numbers or for meanings, the tombs that returned older copies, to the translations into Latin, English and German. Each node says what it changed in the text. Marks: ✔ checked, ○ indirect, ◆ contested, ◇ from memory and still to check.

marks.label: checked: read in the cited source (for Wikipedia, the revision linked)
indirect: a source that summarises another, or a lead paragraph only
from memory, not yet checked against a source

nodes.name: Numbers on bone and bronze (before c. 1000 BCE)

metadata.when: Late Shang into the Western Zhou; the dated pieces run from about 1300 to 700 BCE, and this item treats the older ones (before about 1000 BCE) ✔

sections.What it is: Groups of numbers, mostly in sixes and sometimes in threes, cut or written on oracle bones, bronzes, pottery and other objects from the late Shang and the Western Zhou. Scholars read them as the results of casts ✔ [@breard_cook2020] [@nielsen1990]: the raw material out of which line figures were later drawn.
sections.What it changed in the text: Almost no text yet: the number-groups are only occasionally followed by a word or a short omen, as on a few oracle bones ✔ [@nielsen1990] [@breard_cook2020]. Scholars who read the number-groups as ancestors of the hexagrams take odd numbers as solid lines and even numbers as broken ones, but they disagree on how the lines came from the numbers: Zhang Zhenglang held that the numerals narrowed over time to one odd and one even sign, and Nielsen suggests the solid line grew from 1 and the broken one from 6, while Ding Sixin argues from the Tsinghua Shifa that the lines come from 7 (written like 1) and 8, set by the stalk method, and calls the narrowing theory wrong ◆ [@nielsen1990] [@ding2018]. On the bones and bronzes the numbers are mostly 1, 5, 6, 7 and 8, with 9 rare; the four values 6, 7, 8 and 9 belong to the later stalk method ✔ [@nielsen1990] [@breard_cook2020].
sections.The record: In the hexagrams, broken lines stand for the stalk values 6 and 8 and solid lines for 7 and 9 ✔ [@wp_iching]; the stalk method that yields only 6 to 9 is described from the second or first century BCE ✔ [@breard_cook2020]. That the number-groups on bones and bronzes are ancestors of the hexagrams is the reading most scholars have followed since 1980, but it has been questioned: it assumes early diviners read odd and even numbers as yang and yin, which the early material does not show, and a few scholars have denied that the groups are hexagram-like figures at all ◆ [@breard_cook2020] [@ding2018]. The reading was worked out by Zhang Zhenglang, in a lecture at a palaeography conference in Changchun in early December 1978 and in print in 1980 (Kaogu xuebao 1980, no. 4); Li Xueqin had remarked in 1956 that such numerals recall the 'nine' and 'six' of the Zhouyi ✔ [@nielsen1990] [@ding2018] [@zhang_lunyi2011]. The date here is a range, not a find.

nodes.name: Zhouyi, the Changes of Zhou (c. 825 BCE)

metadata.when: Western Zhou; compiled c. 825 BCE (Shaughnessy's dating)

sections.What it is: The core: 64 figures, each with a name, a short judgment, and six line statements. A diviner's handbook in Early Old Chinese. It says nothing about its own origin [@wp_iching].
sections.What it changed in the text: This is the layer every later book changes. Tradition credited it to King Wen and the Duke of Zhou (and the trigrams to Fu Xi); Shaughnessy's influential dating puts its compilation in the late 9th century BCE, from its language set beside the Classic of Poetry and dated bronze inscriptions; other modern estimates run from the 10th to the 4th century BCE [@wp_iching; @shaughnessy2022].
sections.The record: Dating by Shaughnessy to the last quarter of the 9th century BCE ✔ [@wp_iching; @shaughnessy2022], from [@shaughnessy1983] (not opened). Modern estimates range from the 10th to the 4th century BCE ✔ [@wp_iching]. The traditional authorship is 'no longer generally accepted' ✔ [@wp_iching].

nodes.name: Divinations in the Zuozhuan and Guoyu

metadata.when: Accounts set about 672–485 BCE (sources differ by a year or two); the Zuozhuan largely complete by about 300 BCE, the Guoyu put together from the 5th to the late 4th century BCE ◆

sections.What it is: Two histories that record more than twenty divinations with the Zhouyi for ruling houses ✔ [@wp_iching]; Kidder Smith counts about two dozen references to the Zhouyi or stalk divination in the Zuozhuan, two-thirds of them efforts to interpret its figures and line statements [@smith1989]. Wikipedia calls them the oldest descriptions of divination with the book ✔ [@wp_iching].
sections.What it changed in the text: They show the text read without a fixed commentary: the diviners work from the figure, its trigrams and its line statements, and sometimes argue over the meaning ✔ [@wp_iching] [@smith1989]. In all twelve line statements quoted, the original hexagram supplies the line ✔ [@wp_iching]. Kidder Smith, whose reading Shaughnessy reached independently, takes the word zhi in 'X zhi Y' as 'of', naming one line, and notes that the 'changing into' reading goes back at least to the Western Han; the idea of changing lines turning one hexagram into another is a later reading ✔ [@smith1989]. Smith also counts six cases, sixty percent of his examples, in which the diviner reads the second hexagram as well, and sees in this how the later reading grew [@smith1989].
sections.The record: Accounts dated 671–487 BCE for the divinations in one source, and 672–485 BCE for all references to the Zhouyi or stalk divination in Kidder Smith's count ◆ [@wp_iching] [@smith1989]; no changing lines in them, on the reading of Shaughnessy and Kidder Smith ✔ [@wp_iching] [@smith1989]. The Zuozhuan was largely complete by about 300 BCE and is usually placed in the 4th century BCE; the Guoyu was put together from the 5th to the late 4th century BCE ✔ [@uwpress_zuo2016] [@wp_zuozhuan] [@wp_guoyu].

metadata.when: Warring States bamboo slips (one radiocarbon date, 305 ± 30 BCE), donated to Tsinghua University in July 2008; the Shifa was published in volume 4, with a December 2013 imprint ✔

sections.What it is: A divination manual among the Tsinghua bamboo slips, a large looted Warring States collection donated to Tsinghua University in 2008 [@wp_tsinghua]. It writes casts as numerals, in groups of three and in side-by-side pairs of six, with 7 written like 1; it has a section on the 'images' of its numeral lines, so its numbers also work as lines ✔ [@tsinghua_ctwx_v4] [@breard_cook2020] [@ding2018].
sections.What it changed in the text: It shows a fourth-century BCE Chu practice of casting and reading number-figures by its own rules: the three-numeral figure is the base unit, and a line's rank in a six-line stack does not matter as it does in the Zhouyi's tradition ✔ [@breard_cook2020]. Its example casts match the numeral records on Chu slips from Tianxingguan, Baoshan and Geling, and paired figures are read by a four-position method, not as an original and a changed hexagram ✔ [@tsinghua_ctwx_v4] [@ding2018]. The same volume's Biegua lists the hexagram names, 64 in all with one of its eight strips lost, in the Mawangdui order ✔ [@tsinghua_ctwx_v4].
sections.The record: The collection, its 2008 acquisition and its looted origin ✔ [@wp_tsinghua] [@li_xueqin2013]. The Shifa appeared in volume 4 of the Tsinghua series, with a December 2013 imprint (Zhongxi Book Co., Shanghai); the volume was presented to the public on 7 January 2014 ✔ [@tsinghua_ctwx_v4] [@zh_tsinghua]. The c. 305 BCE date is the collection's single radiocarbon date (305 ± 30 BCE), taken from blank fragments, so it dates the bamboo, not necessarily the text ✔ [@wp_tsinghua] [@zh_tsinghua]. The Shifa's content: 63 strips setting out the principles and method of stalk divination, with many example casts written as numerals, plus diagrams and tables, among them a diagram of trigram positions that resembles but differs from the later 'Later Heaven' arrangement ✔ [@tsinghua_ctwx_v4] [@li_xueqin2013]. Shaughnessy 2014, cited here before, is about the Shanghai, Wangjiatai and Fuyang manuscripts, not a study of the Shifa [@cup_unearthing].

nodes.name: The Shanghai Museum bamboo Zhouyi (c. 300 BCE)

metadata.when: Warring States (Chu), c. 300 BCE; bought by the Shanghai Museum in 1994 ✔

sections.What it is: The oldest surviving copy of the Zhouyi, on bamboo slips, written around 300 BCE. Bought by the Shanghai Museum in 1994 after the strips turned up on the Hong Kong antiquities market, so the tomb they were taken from is not recorded (probably in Hubei or Hunan) ✔ [@wp_smbs; @zh_smbs; @shaughnessy2005].
sections.What it changed in the text: It shows the text already in its current form by 300 BCE, used at all levels of society, but still with small variations [@wp_iching]. It also carries a pair of symbols, written after the hexagram name and at the end of the hexagram text, whose meaning is unsettled: Shaughnessy judged none of the explanations offered convincing in 2005 ✔ [@shaughnessy2005]. The symbols are black and red ✔ [@shaughnessy2005].
sections.The record: Date and form ✔ [@wp_iching]; Warring States Chu, copied about 300 BCE, bought in 1994 ✔ [@shaughnessy2005; @wp_smbs]. Wikipedia's hexagram section also says the oldest manuscript was 'found in 1987 and now held by the Shanghai Library' ◆ [@wp_iching]. The same article's history section and the museum article date the Shanghai Museum manuscript to 1994 ✔ [@wp_iching; @wp_smbs], as does Shaughnessy's study of it ✔ [@shaughnessy2005]; none of the sources opened here mentions a 1987 find held by the Shanghai Library. The section cites [@shaughnessy2014] pp. 52–53, not opened ◇. It also says that manuscript was 'almost certainly' in the King Wen order, where Shaughnessy 2005 says only that the breaks in the strips may suggest an order more or less like the received one ✔ [@shaughnessy2005]. Provenance from the market ✔ [@wp_smbs; @zh_smbs].

metadata.when: Warring States to early Han; the Great Commentary c. 300 BCE

sections.What it is: Seven commentaries, three of them in two parts, hence ten: on the judgments, on the images, the Great Commentary, the Words on the Text, the Discussion of the Trigrams, the Sequence and the Miscellaneous notes [@wp_iching_de].
sections.What it changed in the text: The biggest change in the book's history. The Wings bring yin and yang (the words do not occur in the Zhouyi), the cosmology of the trigrams, the moral 'superior man' of the Great Images, and the claim that the book is a model of the universe [@wp_iching_de; @wp_iching]. Later editions printed them inside the text, so most readers since have read the oracle through them.
sections.The record: Written in a later language than the Zhouyi, by a different society ✔; origins 'still a mystery' ✔; the Confucius attribution rests on shaky ground ✔ [@wp_iching]. Yin and yang absent from the Zhouyi ✔ [@wp_iching_de].

nodes.name: Guicang, the 'Return to the Hidden' (Wangjiatai copy)

metadata.when: Composition date disputed (a Shang-era origin has been argued, and so has a Warring States date); the copy found was buried in a third-century BCE Qin tomb, excavated in March 1993 ◆

sections.What it is: One of the two other 'Changes' the Rites of Zhou names beside the Zhouyi (the other is the Lianshan), naming their methods rather than a written text. A Guicang listed in the Sui shu survived in part to the Southern Song and was then lost, leaving quotations that Ma Guohan gathered in the Qing; a copy on bamboo turned up in 1993. It pairs hexagrams with stories, such as Chang'e fleeing to the moon after a divination ✔ [@wp_iching] [@zh_guicang] [@hein2019] [@wp_guicang].
sections.What it changed in the text: A different way of attaching words to the 64 figures (the Rites of Zhou gives all three Changes eight trigrams and sixty-four hexagrams): stories in place of the Zhouyi's terse judgments and line statements. The copy found is fragmentary, and its stories are sometimes tied to different hexagrams than in later quotations. It shows several divination traditions ran side by side, and that the Zhouyi's text was one choice among them ✔ [@zh_guicang] [@hein2019] [@wp_guicang].
sections.The record: Named in the Rites of Zhou, whose own date is debated, as one of three Changes ✔ [@wp_iching] [@hein2019]; rediscovered 1993 ✔ [@wp_guicang] (Wikipedia says 'a rural bog'; the find was Qin tomb 15 at Wangjiatai, Jiangling, Hubei, in March 1993: 394 of its 813 slips, which the excavators read as two copies ✔ [@zh_wangjiatai] [@hein2019]). The Guicang copy is thought to date from the end of the Warring States, judged by script close to Chu slips; the slips have since decayed, so this cannot be retested ✔ [@zh_wangjiatai] [@hein2019]. Whether the excavated text is the Guicang the Rites of Zhou meant is ◆ argued: the excavators gave it the title because it parallels quotations of the Guicang in later books, and many scholars accept that, but what kind of Guicang it is, and whether it goes back to a Shang-era Yi or is a Warring States work, remains under discussion; one 2010 article argues, going by its title, that the Wangjiatai hexagrams are neither the Shang 'Yin Yi' nor the Guicang [@hein2019] [@zhu_yuanqing2002] [@ren_liang2002] [@gao_xinhua2021] [@zh_wangjiatai].

metadata.when: Han tomb at Mawangdui, Changsha; excavated 1973; a transcription of the hexagram and line text appeared in 1984, and the manuscript was published in 1993, still incompletely ✔

sections.What it is: A near-complete Zhouyi on silk with commentaries, found in 1973 in a Han tomb [@wp_mawangdui; @wp_iching_de].
sections.What it changed in the text: The hexagrams are in a different order: grouped by upper trigram instead of in the King Wen pairs. At least 560 characters, about 12 % of the readable text, differ from the received version ✔ [@wp_iching_de; @rutt1999], and its commentaries are not the Ten Wings as we have them. One of them shows Confucius valuing the book for wisdom first and divination second [@wp_iching_de; @wp_iching].
sections.The record: Found 1973 ✔ [@wp_mawangdui]; published in 1993, though only in part (a transcription of the hexagram and line text had appeared in 1984, photographs in 1992) ✔ [@shaughnessy1994; @rutt1999]; 12 % variant characters, different order ✔ [@wp_iching_de]; the Confucius commentary ✔ [@wp_iching]. Tomb sealed 168 BCE, the silk copied about 175 BCE ✔ [@wp_mawangdui; @wp_mawangdui_site; @shaughnessy1994]. First English translation of the Mawangdui texts: Shaughnessy's, for Ballantine, which calls itself so in its subtitle ○ [@shaughnessy1997; @cup_unearthing; @rutt1999]. Its year is 1997 in the catalogue record and in Rutt's review, 1996 in Shaughnessy's own 2005 notes ◆ [@shaughnessy1997; @rutt1999; @shaughnessy2005].

metadata.when: Early Han tomb at Shuanggudui, Fuyang (Anhui); excavated 1977 ✔

sections.What it is: Fragments of the Zhouyi on bamboo from an early Han tomb, found in 1977 [@wp_iching_de].
sections.What it changed in the text: Nearly two thirds of the characters (2,009 of 3,119) are formulaic divination statements found neither in the received text nor in the Mawangdui copy ✔ [@wp_shuanggudui; @shaughnessy2001]: a copy used as a divination manual, with at least one divination statement attached to each hexagram and line statement ✔ [@shaughnessy2001]. The matters they cover include illness, marriage, pregnancy and births, crime, imprisonment, flight and military action, serving a lord, taking office, travel, hunting and fishing, and the weather ✔ [@shaughnessy2001].
sections.The record: Found 1977 at Shuanggudui ✔ [@wp_iching_de]. The tomb is Xiahou Zao's, second lord of Ruyin, who died in 165 BCE, so it is thought to have been sealed that year; the Changes survives in 752 fragments with 3,119 characters, of which 1,110 are the Zhouyi text itself ✔ [@wp_shuanggudui; @shaughnessy2001].

nodes.name: The Classic of Changes (Han canon, 136 BCE)

metadata.when: 136 BCE, Emperor Wu of Han (the traditional date); carved in stone in the Xiping Stone Classics, 175–183 CE ✔

sections.What it is: In 136 BCE Emperor Wu is said to have raised the Five Classics to official standing, the Zhou yi among them ✔ [@nylan2001; @wp_iching; @smith2012]. Wikipedia adds that he named it 'the first among the classics', but Western Han lists usually put the Changes fourth, and the Changes-first order appears only from the Eastern Han ◆ [@wp_iching; @wp_fbfc; @nylan2001]. From then on it is the Yijing, the Classic of Changes, bound to the Ten Wings ✔ [@wp_iching].
sections.What it changed in the text: One standard version, with the Wings, is carved in stone as one of the Xiping Stone Classics and becomes the received text for over two thousand years, until the excavated copies came back ✔ [@wp_iching; @wp_xiping]. A surviving fragment of the stone Changes, now in the Xi'an Beilin, carries the end of the Great Commentary, the Words on the Text and the Discussion of the Trigrams on its back ✔ [@zh_beilin]. The carving did not fix the texts or end the disputes over them ✔ [@nylan2001]. The variants in the manuscripts above are what this standard text smoothed away.
sections.The record: 136 BCE and the Five Classics ✔; the Xiping Stone Classics ✔ [@wp_iching]. The German article dates the oldest stone witness to a stele at Luoyang of 171 CE ◆ [@wp_iching_de]. Nylan has the emperor order the stone classics in 172 CE, and the English, Chinese and German list articles give 175 for the start of the carving ✔ [@nylan2001; @wp_xiping; @zh_xiping; @de_steinklassiker], so 171 looks like an outlier; its source, Schilling p. 371, was not opened ◇. The Xiping carving ran from 175 to 183 CE ✔ [@wp_xiping; @zh_xiping; @nylan2001].

metadata.when: Western Han, 1st century BCE (in office from 45 BCE, executed 37 BCE) ✔

sections.What it is: Jing Fang, also a music theorist and astronomer [@wp_jingfang], read the hexagrams against the calendar [@hanshu75], the musical pitches [@zh_jingfang] and the stems and branches ◆ [@ck_jingshi; @smith2009_paper; @zh_jingfang]: the 'images and numbers' school [@wp_iching].
sections.What it changed in the text: The eight 'palaces' of the 64, with each line tied to times and elements, are traditionally his [@sep_change; @smith2009_paper] ◆: ChinaKnowledge describes him as extending what his teacher Jiao Yanshou taught on the palaces and on najia, the pairing of hexagrams with the celestial stems [@ck_jingshi], and one study argues they came from another school (Xun Shuang, Yu Fan, Gan Bao) and were credited to him through the Jingshi yizhuan [@zh_jingfang]. Most of his writing is lost. The Jingshi yizhuan survives under his name [@zh_jingfang; @ck_jingshi], and fragments of Han image-and-number commentary survive in the Tang anthology Zhou yi jijie [@wp_iching; @sep_change].
sections.The record: Most of the Han image-and-number commentary, Jing Fang's included, is lost; short fragments survive in the Tang anthology Zhou yi jijie ✔ [@wp_iching; @sep_change]. A work called the Jingshi yizhuan survives under his name [@zh_jingfang; @ck_jingshi]. His dates: 77–37 BCE [@zh_jingfang; @sep_change; @ck_jingshi], 78–37 BCE [@wp_jingfang] ◆. The Hanshu gives the year of his execution (Jianzhao 2, 37 BCE) and his age at death, 41, but no birth year [@hanshu75; @hanshu9]. The eight palaces ◆ (above).

metadata.when: First draft completed 2 BCE on the dating of Nylan and co-authors; Yang Xiong was at work on it under Emperor Ai (7–1 BCE) ○

sections.What it is: A new divination classic written to stand beside the Changes [@wp_taixuan]: 81 figures of four lines with three values each, instead of 64 figures of six lines with two ✔ [@wp_taixuan; @hanshu87].
sections.What it changed in the text: Not an edit of the Changes but an imitation of it: proof that, by the end of the Western Han, the form of the book could be copied and redesigned.
sections.The record: Composed by Yang Xiong, first draft 2 BCE ○ [@wp_taixuan; @unicode_taixuan]; the text survives in editions with the commentary of Fan Wang (Jin dynasty) and of Sima Guang (Song) ✔ [@wp_taixuan; @unicode_taixuan]. The 81 tetragrams ✔ [@wp_taixuan; @hanshu87; @unicode_taixuan].

nodes.name: Wang Bi, Commentary on the Zhouyi (3rd century)

metadata.when: Wang Bi lived 226–249; Han Kangbo (332–380 in two sources, c. 335–c. 385 in another) later wrote the commentary on the Xici, Shuogua, Xugua and Zagua ✔

sections.What it is: A short, sharp commentary by a philosopher who died at 23 [@wp_wangbi], or at 24 in He Shao's count [@sanguozhi28]. It set aside the Han numerology [@wangbi_lueli; @sep_change] and read the Ten Wings' philosophy straight into the hexagrams [@wp_iching].
sections.What it changed in the text: The words now matter more than the numbers: 'meanings and principles' over 'images and numbers'. Once you have the meaning, he argued, you can forget the image ✔ [@wangbi_lueli; @sep_change]. Han Kangbo's commentary on the Xici, Shuogua, Xugua and Zagua, joined to Wang Bi's on the hexagram and line texts, Tuan, Xiang and Wenyan, makes the Zhouyi zhu, the edition later orthodoxy built on [@wp_shisanjing; @ck_wujingzhengyi; @wp_iching].
sections.The record: ✔ [@wp_wangbi; @wp_iching]. 'Forget the image once you have the meaning' paraphrases a passage in his Zhouyi lüeli, the chapter 'Mingxiang' ('Clarifying the images'), where words and images are compared to a rabbit snare and a fish trap ✔ [@wangbi_lueli; @sep_change]. English: Richard John Lynn, The Classic of Changes (Columbia University Press, 1994) ✔ [@lynn1994]. The timeline's year for the commentary, 245, is an estimate within his lifetime: no source opened dates it ◇.

nodes.name: Kong Yingda, The Correct Meaning of the Zhouyi (7th century)

metadata.when: Tang; compiled under Emperor Taizong from the late 630s, revised under Emperor Gaozong and promulgated in 653 ✔

sections.What it is: The Tang court's official edition: the Zhouyi zhu of Wang Bi and Han Kangbo with a further sub-commentary, Kong Yingda leading the editors [@wp_iching; @zh_wujing; @ck_wujingzhengyi; @wp_shisanjing].
sections.What it changed in the text: Orthodoxy by decree. It became the standard edition through the Song [@wp_iching]; from 653 the court had the yearly mingjing examination follow it [@jiutangshu4; @tanghuiyao77], and knowledge of Wang Bi's commentary was tested in the civil-service examinations through the Tang and Song [@sep_change; @wp_iching_de].
sections.The record: Ordered by Taizong, based on Wang Bi's commentary, standard through the Song ✔ [@wp_iching; @jiutangshu73]; tested in the civil-service examinations ✔ [@wp_iching_de; @sep_change]. The Tang huiyao dates the first compilation (170 juan, called Yizan) to 638 and the presentation of the revised text to 653, the year the Jiu Tangshu has it issued to the realm [@tanghuiyao77; @jiutangshu4]. For 642 the accounts differ ◆: Chinese Wikipedia has the work written up that year [@zh_wujing], while Japanese Wikipedia, following Fukushima (1973), has a second compilation begun then [@ja_wujing]; English Wikipedia gives 637 and five years' work [@wp_kongyingda].

metadata.when: Northern Song; Shao Yong lived 1011–1077 (born late in the Chinese year 1011, on a day that fell in January 1012) ✔

sections.What it is: Shao Yong [@wp_shaoyong] is credited with an order of the hexagrams that reads like binary numbers, called the 'Earlier Heaven' (xiantian, also rendered 'Prior to Heaven') or Fu Xi sequence; the diagram handed down from him sets the 64 hexagrams in a circle with a square inside it ✔ [@wp_iching; @wp_kingwen; @adler_zhuxi_yi; @benyi_siku; @wang_maohong].
sections.What it changed in the text: Not a change in the words but in the arrangement: an order the Zhouyi never had, attributed back to the legendary Fu Xi. This is the order that reached Leibniz [@wp_iching].
sections.The record: Shao Yong lived 1011–1077 ✔ [@lc_shaoyong; @wp_shaoyong]; he was born on the 25th day of the twelfth month of the Chinese year 1011, which fell on 21 January 1012, and some works give 1012–1077 [@zh_shaoyong; @wp_shaoyong]. The binary-like order, which he did not intend mathematically ✔ [@wp_iching]; it reached Leibniz through Bouvet, after Leibniz had worked out binary himself in the 1670s ✔ [@strickland_numsys] (see Bouvet and Leibniz). The diagrams' names and the attribution to Fu Xi ◆: Shao Yong, as Zhu Xi's Qimeng quotes him, calls the Shuogua passage on Heaven and Earth fixing their places Fu Xi's eight trigrams, and the Benyi as printed labels four diagrams 'Fu Xi's' and traces them through Li Zhicai, Mu Xiu and Chen Tuan [@benyi_siku; @hu_wei_yitu]; Qing critics held that they are Shao's own learning, not Fu Xi's [@siku_yitu_tiyao; @wang_maohong]. Their Daoist pedigree was argued first by Yuan and Ming writers and then by Qing scholars, Hu Wei among them ✔ [@siku_yitu_tiyao; @hu_wei_yitu] (see Hu Wei).

nodes.name: Cheng Yi, Commentary on the Changes (c. 1099)

metadata.when: Northern Song; preface dated 1099 (Yuanfu 2) ✔

sections.What it is: A Neo-Confucian commentary that reads the book as a guide to moral perfection and to honest government [@wp_iching].
sections.What it changed in the text: The figures become lessons for ministers: how to form factions honestly, root out corruption, solve problems in government [@wp_iching]. Divination recedes further: he follows Wang Bi's text, sets each hexagram's Xugua line at its head, comments on the judgments and images in terms of principle rather than Shao Yong's numbers, and writes nothing on the Xici, Shuogua or Zagua ✔ [@yichuan_siku; @adler_zhuxi_yi].
sections.The record: Content ✔ [@wp_iching]. The 1099 preface date ✔ [@cheng_yizhuan; @yichuan_siku]. Whether Cheng Yi finished the commentary is ◆: Yang Shi's postscript and a late letter of Cheng Yi's say it was left unfinished and that pupils put the text together after his death in 1107, while Zhu Xi's chronology says he had finished it [@cheung2021; @yichuan_siku]; one recent translation says only that he composed or at least completed it during his first exile [@adler_review_harrington].

nodes.name: Zhu Xi, The Original Meaning of the Zhouyi (12th century)

metadata.when: Southern Song; Zhu Xi lived 1130–1200; the Benyi dated 1188 in Adler's recent work (after Shu Jingnan), 1177 in the older consensus ◆

sections.What it is: Zhu Xi [@wp_zhuxi] argued that the book was first of all for divination, and that divination could serve moral self-cultivation. He also reconstructed the yarrow-stalk method from the Xici's sketch, setting it out in the Yixue qimeng ✔ [@wp_iching; @adler2021_divination].
sections.What it changed in the text: Two lasting changes. First, nine diagrams printed at the head of the Benyi, among them four 'Fu Xi' diagrams whose note credits them to Shao Yong ◆: they stand there in the Song print of 1265 [@benyi_siku], but whether Zhu Xi or a follower put them there is disputed [@adler_zhuxi_yi; @wang_maohong]. Second, a reconstructed yarrow method, still the standard way to cast today [@wp_iching]: the 'traditional' method is a 12th-century reconstruction. A Yuan decree of 1313 named the commentaries of Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi as the main ones for the Changes in the classics essay set for Han and southern candidates, with the first examinations set for 1314–15 ✔ [@yuanshi81] (the Wikipedia lead gives 1313 for his Four Books commentaries [@wp_zhuxi]).
sections.The record: Synthesis of both Han lines, divination plus self-cultivation, the yarrow reconstruction ✔ [@wp_iching]. Title and the primer's date ✔ (Zhouyi benyi; a separate primer, the Yixue qimeng, on the diagrams, the numbers and yarrow divination, with a preface dated 1186) [@adler2021_divination; @qimeng_preface]. Zhu Xi lived 1130–1200 ✔ [@wp_zhuxi; @adler2021_divination]; the Benyi is dated 1188 in Adler's recent work (after Shu Jingnan), 1177 in the older consensus ◆ [@adler_zhuxi_yi; @adler2021_divination; @wang_maohong]. The Qing Siku editors report that the Song history gives the first draft of the Yixue qimeng to Cai Yuanding ○ [@siku_yitu_tiyao].

metadata.when: Bouvet in Beijing writes to Leibniz in November 1701; Leibniz writes his paper on binary arithmetic in April 1703 and it is printed in 1705 ✔

sections.What it is: Joachim Bouvet, a French Jesuit at the Kangxi court and the leading Figurist, studied the I Ching and corresponded with Leibniz [@wp_bouvet]. Bouvet, who had learned Leibniz's binary notation, matched it to the arrangement of the hexagrams called Fuxi's (a reordering credited to Shao Yong), and Leibniz took up the match ✔ [@strickland_numsys; @leibniz1703].
sections.What it changed in the text: The hexagrams were already in European print: Leibniz had seen the King Wen order in a Latin book about Confucius, Confucius Sinarum philosophus (Intorcetta and others, Paris 1687) ✔ [@strickland_numsys]. His 1703 paper takes Fuxi's figures as confirming his own binary ✔ [@leibniz1703], and has been described as the first European commentary on the I Ching ○ [@wp_iching]. Bouvet sought in it the truths of Christianity, known in ancient times [@wp_bouvet]. Leibniz found binary numbers in it. Leibniz worked from diagrams of the hexagram order, and his paper dismisses the Chinese commentaries as chasing far-fetched meanings ✔ [@leibniz1703; @strickland_numsys]; Bouvet had studied the Yijing for years and suspected it held a number-based metaphysics ✔ [@strickland_numsys].
sections.The record: Bouvet, Figurism, the correspondence ✔ [@wp_bouvet]; Bouvet's match of binary to Shao Yong's order, and Leibniz's own binary, which dates from the 1670s ✔ [@strickland_numsys; @strickland_lewis2022]. Bouvet's letter of November 1701 and Leibniz's 'Explication de l'arithmétique binaire', dated 7 April 1703 and printed in the Académie's volume for 1703, which appeared in 1705 ✔ [@strickland_lewis2022; @strickland_numsys; @leibniz1703].

metadata.when: Qing, 1706 ✔

sections.What it is: Hu Wei (1633–1714), classicist and geographer, wrote the Yitu mingbian, 'Clarifying the Diagrams of the Changes' ✔ [@zh_huwei]: a study that sets old texts against each other to trace the Song diagrams to Chen Tuan and the Daoist arts of cultivation and number-lore, not to Fu Xi ✔ [@skqs_yitumingbian; @skqs_zongmu_006].
sections.What it changed in the text: The diagrams at the front of the classic were late additions, not ancient revelation: a doubt Hu Wei did not start (Song critics, the Yuan writer Chen Yingrun, and early Qing writers such as Huang Zongxi, Huang Zongyan and Mao Qiling had raised it), though the Siku editors say he traced it to its sources more fully ✔ [@skqs_zongmu_006; @skqs_yitumingbian]. The Qing classicist Pi Xirui credited it with refuting the River Chart and the Luo Writing, while noting that on the Hongfan it also attacked Han scholars ✔ [@pi_jingxue_lishi; @zh_huwei]. Qing scholars more generally turned to the old language of the text [@wp_iching].
sections.The record: The Qing turn to pre-classical grammar ✔ [@wp_iching]. Hu Wei, his dates and the title ✔ [@zh_huwei]; the year 1706, from his own preface and from Henderson's chapter ✔ [@skqs_yitumingbian; @henderson1994]; the Daoist origin of the diagrams and the earlier critics, from the Siku editors' notes ✔ [@skqs_zongmu_006; @skqs_yitumingbian]; Pi Xirui's verdict ✔ [@pi_jingxue_lishi].

nodes.name: The Kangxi Emperor's Balanced Annotations on the Zhouyi (1715)

metadata.when: Qing, 1715 ✔

sections.What it is: An imperial compendium, the Zhouyi zhezhong ('Balanced Annotations'), compiled under Li Guangdi as chief editor, with a staff of proofreaders, section compilers and copyists named in the book ✔ [@skqs_zhezhong; @wp_li_guangdi], which printed the Classic proper and the Ten Wings in separate sections, as the old text had them ✔ [@zhezhong_fanli; @hon2005; @legge1882_scan], and puts Zhu Xi's Original Meaning and Cheng Yi's Commentary first, then comments from other scholars, Han to Ming, then the compilers' own judgments, with the Kangxi Emperor's views among them ✔ [@zhezhong_fanli; @skqs_zhezhong; @legge1882_scan]. The Kangxi Emperor was especially fond of the I Ching and ordered new interpretations [@wp_iching].
sections.What it changed in the text: The edition Wilhelm translated from ✔ [@de_wilhelm; @hon2005]: the Song reading, now with an emperor's seal. Legge used it too: his preface records his debt to the imperial edition of 1715, and his notes cite its editors throughout ✔ [@legge1882_scan; @hon2005].
sections.The record: Kangxi's interest in the I Ching ✔ [@wp_iching], and his own preface naming Li Guangdi and dated 1715 ✔ [@skqs_zhezhong]. Title ✔ [@wp_li_guangdi]; Li Guangdi as chief editor ✔ [@skqs_zhezhong]; Wilhelm's use ✔ [@de_wilhelm; @hon2005]; the year 1715 ✔ [@skqs_zhezhong; @skqs_zongmu_006; @legge1882_scan]; Legge's use ✔ [@legge1882_scan; @hon2005].

nodes.name: Liu Yiming, a Daoist reading of the Zhouyi (late 18th century)

metadata.when: Qing; Liu Yiming lived 1734–1821; the commentary dates from the late 1790s (1796 or 1798) ◆

sections.What it is: A master of Daoist inner alchemy [@wp_liuyiming] who read the hexagrams in order as one course of inner cultivation, in two strands, one advancing the yang fire and one circulating the yin tally: Qian opens the first, Kun the second, and each later hexagram follows on from the one two places before it ✔ [@liu_chanzhen_text].
sections.What it changed in the text: The same lines, a different body: Liu's own preface says the Yi is not a book of divination but a study of principle, nature and destiny ✔ [@liu_chanzhen_text]; the Zhezhong editors describe Cheng Yi's reading as one about cultivating the self, ordering the household and governing the state ✔ [@zhezhong_fanli]. His Zhouyi chanzhen, 'Uncovering the True in the Book of Changes', reached English as Thomas Cleary's The Taoist I Ching (1986), which leaves out the book's opening chapter of charts ✔ [@wp_liuyiming; @cleary1986; @pregadio2025].
sections.The record: Liu Yiming, his dates and his Longmen lineage ✔ [@wp_liuyiming]. The commentary's title and its English translation ✔ [@wp_liuyiming]; its date is given as 1796 in the publisher's description of the English edition and as 1798 in Liu's own preface ◆ [@ol_taoist_iching; @liu_chanzhen_text].

nodes.name: Régis and others, the Latin Y-King (made c. 1730s; printed 1834)

metadata.when: Translated in Beijing in the early 18th century; edited by Julius Mohl, Stuttgart, 1834

sections.What it is: The first translation into a Western language, by the Jesuit Jean-Baptiste Régis, who also mapped China for the Kangxi Emperor. It waited a century to be printed [@wp_regis].
sections.What it changed in the text: Latin, with long prolegomena on Chinese ideas of God and spirits that Legge later praised [@wp_regis]. The translation was a joint Jesuit work: the 1834 preface says Joseph de Mailla rendered the Chinese word for word into Latin, checking it against the Manchu version, and Pierre du Tartre explained the text from history ✔ [@regis1834].
sections.The record: First Westerner to translate it; Mohl's Stuttgart edition of 1834 ✔ [@wp_regis] (from the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, which quotes Legge). The title page: 'ex latina interpretatione P. Regis aliorumque ex Soc. Jesu P.P.', edited by Julius Mohl, Stuttgart and Tübingen, Cotta, 1834 ✔ [@regis1834].

metadata.when: Shanghai, 1876 ✔

sections.What it is: An English translation six years before Legge's, called the first complete English translation ✔ [@li2022; @yang2020], by Thomas McClatchie, a Church Missionary Society (Anglican) missionary in Shanghai, sent out in 1844 and in China from 1845 ✔ [@wp_cms_china].
sections.What it changed in the text: It read the book through comparative mythology ○ [@mcclatchie_chapter], taking Qian and Kun, the first two hexagrams, as the male and female sexual organs ✔ [@legge1882_scan; @sun2025] and tracing the book to Noah's sons and Babel ○ [@yang2020; @smith2012], an approach Legge called unnecessary and its findings unpleasant ✔ [@legge1882_scan]. It's a good example of a translation telling you more about its century than about the Zhou.
sections.The record: A Translation of the Confucian [Yih king], or the 'Classic of Change', with Notes and Appendix (the bracketed romanisation is the cataloguer's), Shanghai, American Presbyterian Mission Press, 1876, catalogued from the 1973 Taipei reprint; xiii, xvii, 455 pages, Chinese and English on facing pages ✔ [@stanford_mcclatchie; @hathi_mcclatchie]; HathiTrust counts x preliminary pages, not xiii [@hathi_mcclatchie]. His keys: the first two hexagrams read as sexual organs ✔ [@legge1882_scan], and the book traced to Noah's sons and Babel ○ [@yang2020; @smith2012]. Legge's response, in his preface (p. xvii) and in a note at pp. 396-397 ✔ [@legge1882_scan]. That it derives from the Kangxi edition ◇: McClatchie cites an 'Imp. Ed.' for a comment ○ [@legge1882_scan], but he printed Appendixes I, II and IV under the Text, as the ordinary school editions do, while the 1715 imperial edition keeps them apart ✔ [@legge1899_scan].

nodes.name: Legge, The Yî King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882)

metadata.when: Oxford, 1882 (2nd ed. 1899) ✔

sections.What it is: James Legge, missionary and Oxford's first professor of Chinese, translated it for Max Müller's Sacred Books of the East [@wp_legge; @legge1882].
sections.What it changed in the text: Legge printed the Zhouyi and the Wings apart (the Text, then the Appendixes), not woven together ✔ [@legge1899_scan]. Words he added to make the terse Chinese read as English sit in parentheses ✔ [@legge1899_scan]: the '(we see its subject as)' you meet on every line here. By his own account he aimed to give the meaning exactly and concisely, holding a literal version to be in vain ✔ [@legge1899_scan]. It reads as Victorian and moralising, and it is public domain; that last point is why it is the text of this library [@repo_changelog].
sections.The record: Legge, the SBE series 1879–1891 ✔ [@wp_legge]; the text ✔ (it is in this library) [@legge1882]. That he used the Kangxi compendium ✔ [@legge1899_scan]: his preface thanks the great imperial edition first published in 1715, whose authors he calls the Khang-hsi editors. That he drew on Régis ✔ [@legge1899_scan]: his 1854 draft followed Régis's example in being concise, and his notes quote and argue with Régis's renderings; he also says that draft proved of no service, so the tie is that he consulted Régis, not that he built on him.
sections.In this library: This node has its own book here: open it from the link below, or from the timeline and the genealogy. (The 64 Hexagrams (Legge))

nodes.name: Wilhelm, I Ging: Das Buch der Wandlungen (1924)

metadata.when: Jena, 1924; made with the scholar Lao Naixuan, finished in Beijing ✔

sections.What it is: Richard Wilhelm, missionary and sinologist, lived 25 years in China. His German I Ching is still counted among the finest translations [@wp_wilhelm].
sections.What it changed in the text: He translated from the Kangxi-era Zhouyi zhezhong ✔ [@de_wilhelm; @wilhelm1924_intro], set most of the Wings under the hexagrams they comment on, and added a commentary excerpted from the main Chinese commentators, with his own Western parallels marked as his ✔ [@wilhelm1924_intro]. That this follows the Song 'meanings and principles' line he learned from his teacher ◇. The result reads as wisdom literature: the voice most Western readers think of as 'the I Ching'.
sections.The record: Wilhelm's life and the translation's standing ✔; Jung was a friend ✔ [@wp_wilhelm]. Jena, Eugen Diederichs, 1924, in two volumes ✔ [@wp_iching_de; @hathi_wilhelm1924]. English Wikipedia's Translations section gives 1923, while its own list of translations in that section gives 1924; Wilhelm's preface is dated Peking, summer 1923 ✔ [@wp_iching; @wilhelm1924_intro]. Made over nearly ten years, mostly in Qingdao with his teacher Lao Naixuan (who died in 1921), and finished in Beijing in 1923 ✔ [@wilhelm1924_intro; @de_wilhelm; @wp_lao_naixuan].

nodes.name: Gushi bian, vol. 3 (1931): the Zhouyi as a Zhou diviner's book

metadata.when: Republican China, 1931 ✔

sections.What it is: The 'Doubting Antiquity' scholars [@wp_doubting] read the classics as historical documents. Their Gushi bian, 'Debates on Ancient History', ran to seven volumes from 1926 ✔ [@wp_gujiegang]. Its third volume (1931) has two parts, one on the Yijing and one on the Shijing ✔ [@richter1993] [@nlc_gushibian3]: fourteen papers on the Zhouyi, opening with Gu Jiegang's study of the stories in its line statements and including Yu Yongliang's and Li Jingchi's discussions of its date and its divination terms ✔ [@nlc_gushibian3] [@shaughnessy2022] [@zh_gushibian], and fifty on the Poetry ✔ [@nlc_gushibian3]. Gu Jiegang, Yu Yongliang and Li Jingchi each placed the hexagram and line statements in the early Western Zhou, and the volume reads the book as a diviners' manual rather than a sacred text and takes up the Wings in separate papers ✔ [@richter1993] [@nlc_gushibian3] [@shaughnessy2022].
sections.What it changed in the text: The layers are pulled apart: the hexagram and line statements are dated early, and the Wings are examined on their own, in at least two papers whose headings say they are not by Confucius ✔ [@nlc_gushibian3]. The sages come out of the authorship: Gu Jiegang denied King Wen the text and still placed it in the early Western Zhou ✔ [@shaughnessy2022], and the Changes' standing as a scripture from Fuxi is challenged in favour of an origin as a diviners' manual ✔ [@richter1993].
sections.The record: The school and its method ✔ [@wp_doubting]. Seven volumes, 1926 to 1941 ✔ [@zh_gushibian] [@richter1993] [@nlc_gushibian1] [@nlc_gushibian7]; the 1944 in the English Wikipedia article on Gu Jiegang cites Richter pp. 370-371, which cover only the first two volumes, and Richter gives 1941 for the last ✔ [@wp_gujiegang] [@richter1993]; volume 3's contributors as the Chinese Wikipedia lists them ✔ [@zh_gushibian], and in its Zhouyi part Gu Jiegang (pp. 1-44), Yu Yongliang (pp. 143-170) and Li Jingchi (pp. 187-251) ✔ [@shaughnessy2022]; volume 3's year (1931) and its two subjects, the Zhouyi and the Poetry ✔ [@richter1993] [@nlc_gushibian3].

nodes.name: Baynes, The I Ching or Book of Changes (1950), with Jung's foreword

metadata.when: Bollingen Series XIX, 1950 ✔

sections.What it is: Cary F. Baynes, a Jungian, translated Wilhelm's German into English [@wp_baynes], with a foreword by C. G. Jung.
sections.What it changed in the text: A translation of a translation. Jung's foreword reframed the casts as synchronicity ✔ [@jung1949; @wp_iching], and Wilhelm's book, in this English edition, reached the 1960s counterculture ✔ [@wp_iching; @smith2012]. It is still in copyright: in September 2026 this library found Wilhelm/Baynes wording in one of its grammars and replaced it with Legge [@repo_changelog].
sections.The record: Baynes translated Wilhelm ✔ [@wp_baynes]; Bollingen XIX, © 1950 ✔ [@repo_changelog]. Jung's foreword (dated Zurich, 1949; pp. xxi-xxxix) ✔ [@jung1949; @sun2025] sets the casts within his idea of synchronicity ✔ [@jung1949; @wp_iching].

nodes.name: Chance and the counterculture: Cage (1951), Dick (1962)

metadata.when: John Cage, Music of Changes, 1951; Philip K. Dick, The Man in the High Castle, 1962

sections.What it is: A composer cast the I Ching to make music ✔ [@wp_music_of_changes], and a novelist put it inside his story ✔ [@wp_high_castle]; that Dick, by his own account, threw coins whenever a character consulted the oracle and let the hexagram lines steer the book, and said he did this only for that book ✔ [@pkd_vertex1974] [@pkd_sfr1976].
sections.What it changed in the text: For Cage the book becomes a source of chance: its 64 hexagrams pick cells in 8-by-8 charts of sounds, durations and dynamics ✔ [@wp_music_of_changes]. For Dick the lines themselves steered the plot: when a character consulted the oracle he threw the coins, wrote down the lines that came, and followed them ✔ [@pkd_vertex1974] [@pkd_sfr1976].
sections.The record: Music of Changes (1951), composed by applying I Ching decisions to charts of sounds, durations and dynamics ✔ [@wp_music_of_changes]. The Man in the High Castle (1962), with the I Ching in its story and among Dick's inspirations ✔ [@wp_high_castle].

nodes.name: Shaughnessy, The Composition of the Zhouyi (1983)

metadata.when: Stanford PhD dissertation, 1983 ✔

sections.What it is: A study of the Zhouyi's date that its author later called an attempt at a comprehensive one: rhyme and four-character phrasing set beside the Classic of Poetry, vocabulary set beside dated Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, and a date in the last two decades of the 9th century BCE, early in King Xuan's reign ✔ [@shaughnessy2022] [@wp_iching]. Lu Kanru and Li Jingchi had compared the text with the Poetry before, and Chen Mengjia with bronze inscriptions ✔ [@shaughnessy2022]. Shaughnessy is a historian of the Zhou and of the Changes [@wp_shaughnessy].
sections.What it changed in the text: No new words, a new date: the last two decades of the 9th century BCE, early in King Xuan's reign ✔ [@shaughnessy2022]. Modern scholars' dates for the text range from the 10th to the 4th century BCE ✔ [@wp_iching]. Its author later wrote that in Western studies this date became more influential than it should have, quoting Kunst and Rutt on roughly 800 BCE, and that the final editing may have come a century or two later ✔ [@shaughnessy2022].
sections.The record: The dating and the method ✔ [@wp_iching] [@shaughnessy2022]; the dissertation's title, department and year ✔ [@sw_shaughnessy1983]; its method and result, as its author summarises them in 2022 ○ [@shaughnessy2022]; the text itself not opened ◇ [@shaughnessy1983].

metadata.when: Ra Uru Hu, 1987 (his account of the origin; first book 1992) ✔

sections.What it is: A modern system that places the 64 hexagrams, which it calls 'gates', on a body chart, and combines them by its own account with astrology, the Kabbalah and the chakra system ✔ [@wp_humandesign; @jovian_ra; @ra_rave_iching]. It isn't a translation, and this library keeps it as a lens.
sections.What it changed in the text: The Judgment, Image and line sayings are replaced by Human Design's own gate themes, line keynotes and commentary; the hexagram titles stay ✔ [@ra_rave_iching]. What carries over is the set of 64 figures under their King Wen numbers (gate 1 is hexagram 1, The Creative) ✔ [@ra_rave_iching]. The King Wen order does not: Ra's wheel runs the gates round the zodiac in another order (25, 17, 21, 51...), each gate spanning 5°37'30" ✔ [@ra_rave_iching]; worked out line by line from the trigrams in [@wp_hexlist], that order is the binary (Fu Xi) sequence [@wp_kingwen] laid round a circle (this library's own check).
sections.The record: Origin story and date as given in this library's Human Design grammar ✔ (its own description); the 1987 experience and the 1992 first book ✔ [@jovian_ra; @wp_humandesign]. Which translation it drew on: the book names none ✔ [@ra_rave_iching]. Its hexagram titles look like the Wilhelm/Baynes English ones; gates 3 and 36, for instance, carry the titles that [@cottrell] quotes from Wilhelm/Baynes ○.
sections.In this library: This node has its own book here: open it from the link below, or from the timeline and the genealogy. (I Ching HD Meta-Categories)

sections.What it is: Translations that read the Zhouyi as a Western Zhou divination text. Redmond translates the Zhouyi alone; Rutt gives it first and puts the Ten Wings in a separate appendix ✔ [@rutt1996; @redmond2017; @lebovitz2018; @biroco_rutt].
sections.What it changed in the text: Both set aside the later moral reading of the Wings, the reverse of Wilhelm, whose pages blend the Zhouyi with the Wings and later commentary: Redmond leaves the Wings out, and Rutt translates them apart from the Zhouyi ✔ [@lebovitz2018; @biroco_rutt]. Both translate words like zhen as an act of divining, not as 'correct and firm' (Legge) or 'perseverance' (Wilhelm/Baynes): Rutt has 'augury', Redmond mostly 'divine', though a reviewer finds him inconsistent ○ [@cottrell; @lebovitz2018].
sections.The record: Titles ✔ [@wp_iching; @rutt_front; @lebovitz2018]: Rutt, The Book of Changes (Zhouyi): A Bronze Age Document (Curzon, Richmond, 1996; paperback RoutledgeCurzon, 2002); Redmond, The I Ching (Book of Changes): A Critical Translation of the Ancient Text (Bloomsbury Academic, 2017). Both name the Western Zhou readings of Shaughnessy (1983) and Richard Kunst (1985) as a base: Rutt says so in his preface, while a reviewer notes Shaughnessy is missing from Redmond's bibliography ○ [@rutt_front; @lebovitz2018].

nodes.name: The excavated texts in English: Mawangdui (1997), Unearthing the Changes (2014)

sections.What it is: English translations of tomb and market manuscripts. The 1997 book gives the Mawangdui silk text and its commentaries (from a tomb of 168 BCE); the 2014 book gives the Shanghai Museum Zhouyi (bought in 1994), the Fuyang Zhouyi (from a tomb) and the Wangjiatai fragments of the Guicang (from a tomb) ✔ [@shaughnessy1997; @shaughnessy2014; @cup_unearthing; @shaughnessy2005; @wp_smbs; @rutt1999].
sections.What it changed in the text: For the first time in English, as the first book's subtitle says, readers can see versions of the book from before the Han canon of 136 BCE fixed it. The Mawangdui text is about 350 years older than any manuscript known before it and arranges the hexagrams in another order ✔ [@rutt1999; @shaughnessy1997]; the Shanghai Museum text, copied about 300 BCE, shows the text was already stable then, with many spelling variants ✔ [@shaughnessy2005]. The first book's jacket calls the find the first new manuscript of the work in two thousand years ○ [@abe_ballantine].
sections.The record: Titles ✔ [@wp_shaughnessy; @shaughnessy1997; @cup_unearthing]: I Ching: The Classic of Changes, subtitled The First English Translation of the Newly Discovered Second-Century B.C. Mawangdui Texts (Ballantine, New York, 1997 ✔ [@shaughnessy1997]; the 1996 in [@wp_iching], which Shaughnessy's own 2005 notes also give [@shaughnessy2005], is not borne out by the catalogue records or two reviews) and Unearthing the Changes: Recently Discovered Manuscripts of the Yi Jing (I Ching) and Related Texts (Columbia University Press, April 2014 ✔ [@cup_unearthing]). The books themselves were not opened.

sections.What it is: This repository: the Legge text split into its layers (the Zhouyi Core, the Ten Wings), the Chinese original, a repair practice, a book you cast, and this tree.
sections.What it changed in the text: It doesn't add a translation. It separates the layers again, keeps the doubts visible with marks, and puts each book's history one tap away.
